title: Lecture 03 - Distributed ID generators: epoch IDs, central ID service, Amazon, Flickr, Snowflake, pagination, Instagram

questions.q: What is the problem statement for ID generation as written on the board?
questions.answer: Assign a globally unique ID to "anything" (object, row, document, event): write a function that spits out something unique every time it is invoked.

questions.q: At the start, is the ID-generating function a central service? Where does it run?
questions.answer: No. It is a function that is part of the application (business) logic, called locally when a request needs an ID; not a central ID service. The central service comes later in the evolution.

questions.q: Why was the current epoch millisecond proposed as the first ID, and under what conditions does it work?
questions.answer: Time is unique and always moves forward, so each invocation seems to get a new value. It works only when there is one machine and the function is never invoked twice within the same millisecond (else go to micro/nanoseconds).

questions.q: Two machines m1 and m2 both call get_id() at epoch ms 1729. What goes wrong with the epoch-ms ID and how is it fixed?
questions.answer: Both return 1729, a collision, so IDs are not globally unique. Fix: concatenate the machine ID with the epoch ms, giving m1-1729 and m2-1729.

questions.q: What general strategy for resolving collisions did the teacher state when adding the machine ID?
questions.answer: Add (concatenate) the thing that led to the collision; since two machines caused it, add the machine ID. A very standard practice.

questions.q: Why can machine_id + epoch ms still collide on a single machine?
questions.answer: If the program has multiple threads (on multiple cores), two threads can invoke the function within the same millisecond and both produce e.g. M1-1729.

questions.q: What two approaches did the board list for handling collisions from threads, in order?
questions.answer: 1. Add thread_id as a differentiator. 2. Add a counter that resets every few minutes (static counter).

questions.q: With the thread-ID approach, what does get_id return and what do IDs look like?
questions.answer: concat(machine_id, thread_id, get_epoch_ms()), e.g. m1-t1-1729, m1-t2-1729, m2-t1-1729.

questions.q: Why prefer a static counter over always appending the thing that caused the collision?
questions.answer: Always appending the cause (machine, thread, ...) leads to gigantic IDs; a single atomically incremented static counter handles any number of threads.

questions.q: What is a static counter and what must be true of its increment?
questions.answer: A globally allocated variable (on the heap) that all threads can access; it is incremented with counter++ every time the function is invoked, and the increment must be atomic/thread-safe (locks, mutex or a native atomic library; it is not atomic by default).

questions.q: With concat(machine_id, epoch_ms, counter++), what sample IDs did the board show for m1?
Why did the teacher say time becomes redundant once a static counter is used, and what was the resulting ID?
questions.answer: Because the counter is atomically incremented on every call, it alone guarantees uniqueness per machine regardless of time; so time was struck out, giving shorter IDs concat(machine_id, counter): m1-01, m1-02, m1-03.

questions.q: What limit does the machine_id + counter approach have?
questions.answer: The counter can hit the integer limit (about 4 billion for 32-bit; 2^64 is massive and you may never hit it). The counter may be reset periodically as long as you don't exceed the limit.

questions.q: What happens to the static counter when the machine or process reboots, and what is the root cause?
questions.answer: The counter resets to 0 and the machine regenerates the same IDs (m1-01, m1-02 ...) it already issued; root cause: the counter is stored in volatile memory with no persistence.

questions.q: What was the first fix for the volatile counter, and how does the code change?
questions.answer: Store the counter to disk (non-volatile) for fault tolerance: counter = load() at startup; in get_id do counter++, save_counter() to disk every time, return concat(machine_id, counter).

questions.q: What two problems does saving the counter to disk on every invocation cause?
questions.answer: 1) Lots of pressure on the disk from many micro disk IOs at high invocation rate; 2) worse latency, since each ID now needs a disk IO instead of being served from memory. (One IO at startup is fine.)

questions.q: A proposal was: at each server startup, read and increment a boot counter, persist it once, and add it as a third part of the ID while the static counter starts from 0. What did the teacher think of it and its downside?
questions.answer: He loved the approach (no per-ID disk writes; each startup gets a new prefix; the startup increment must be atomic), but its downside is a longer ID.

questions.q: What is the 'bank of IDs' / periodic-write idea for reducing disk IO?
questions.answer: Instead of writing on every call, write at a certain frequency: e.g. reserve 1000 ahead and only write again after using them, so disk IOs drop by that factor.

questions.q: Write the flush-frequency version of the counter code as on the board (flush frequency 1000).
questions.answer: counter = load() + 1000; get_id: counter++; if (counter % 1000 == 0) save_counter(); return concat(machine_id, counter).

questions.q: Why must the counter be loaded as load() + flush frequency rather than just load()?
questions.answer: Because IDs generated after the last flush were already used but not persisted; starting from the last saved value would regenerate them (collision). Adding the flush frequency skips past any possibly used IDs.

questions.q: By how much does flushing every 1000 IDs cut disk IO, and how should the periodic write be implemented?
questions.answer: By a factor of 1000. Use a simple mod check (counter % 1000 == 0), not a thread/timer.

questions.q: Flush every 3 values: m1 generates 01..08, flushing at 03 and 06, then crashes after 08. What are the on-disk values and the safe restart value?
questions.answer: On disk: 03, then 06. Safe start = last flushed + flush frequency + 1 = 06 + 3 + 1 = m1-10. Starting at 07 would reissue 07 and 08.

questions.q: In the flush-every-3 example, what is the cost of restarting at the safe value, and why is it acceptable?
questions.answer: Restarting at 10 means some integers (e.g. 09) are never issued — a couple of values are 'leaked'. Acceptable because correctness of the system matters more than utilizing every integer.

questions.q: What two key takeaways/design constraints did the teacher draw from the counter-persistence discussion?
questions.answer: 1) Don't do IO every time; add a periodicity factor (simple mod). 2) When the machine recovers, start from the safest value.

questions.q: Why would anyone need monotonically increasing IDs? Give the teacher's example.
questions.answer: For ordering/conflict resolution: e.g. transactions T1 and T2 from the airline check-in week — the numbers tell which came first, so a 'newer write overrides older write' strategy can accept T2's write.

questions.q: Does monotonically increasing mean strictly sequential? Explain.
questions.answer: No. 1 2 5 7 8 9 32 33 34 is monotonic: each new ID is guaranteed greater than all previous IDs; it needn't be consecutive like 1 2 3 4.

questions.q: How does flipping the order to concat(time, machine_id) help, and what does the board say about time on the LHS?
questions.answer: Time becomes the most significant part, and since time moves forward, IDs are (almost) ordered: 17290001, 17290002, 17300001... Board: all ID generation algorithms have time on the LHS for 'sortability'; LHS decides the order, second half breaks ties.

questions.q: Why is time-first + machine ID not strictly monotonic even with perfect clocks?
questions.answer: Within the same millisecond, the first request might hit machine 2 and the next machine 1, giving 17290002 then 17290001; ordering is only correct across milliseconds.

questions.q: What advantage does time-first ID generation keep despite being only roughly monotonic?
questions.answer: It stays stateless (a request can go to any machine, no central state), giving excellent throughput at minimal cost while being almost monotonic.

questions.q: How do operations teams keep server clocks in sync?
questions.answer: A periodically running job/process syncs each machine's clock with NTP servers; servers commonly go out of sync and it runs more often than you'd think.

questions.q: Why do computer clocks drift?
questions.answer: The clock is a hardware quartz crystal vibrating at a set frequency; heat (e.g. CPU-heavy work) makes it vibrate faster so the clock runs fast; extreme cold makes it slower.

questions.q: Four machines 2, 4, 7, 9 have clocks 23, 24, 23, 23. Requests hit them in that order. What IDs result and what is wrong?
questions.answer: 232, 244, 237, 239 — not monotonically increasing, because of clock skew (machine 4's clock is ahead).

questions.q: What anecdote did the teacher cite about natural phenomena flipping bits?
questions.answer: The 'friendship that made Google special' article: Jeff Dean and Sanjay Ghemawat debugging a bit flipped by a natural phenomenon (solar storm) — you cannot run away from nature.

questions.q: What conclusion did the teacher draw about strict monotonicity when ID logic is distributed?
questions.answer: Ensuring strict monotonicity across distributed systems is practically impossible; too many things (ordering within a ms, clock skew) break it.

questions.q: What is the central ID generation service idea, as drawn?
questions.answer: One ID server; clients (client 1, client 2) make a network call to it, it runs the get_id function and sends the ID back — arrows go up from each client to the ID server and back down.

questions.q: Why does clock skew not break monotonicity on a single machine? What happens when NTP finds the clock ahead?
questions.answer: The clock never goes back in time: if the machine is at 24 but NTP says 23, it slows its counting to let real time catch up rather than jumping back. So a single machine's clock always moves forward.

questions.q: What is the problem with the single central ID server, and the first fix drawn?
questions.answer: It's a single point of failure (ID server or its disk could fail). Fix: multiple ID servers behind a load balancer.

questions.q: With two ID servers behind a load balancer needing monotonic IDs, what must they do and what is the cost?
questions.answer: They must constantly gossip to agree upon the last/next value (converge on an agreed value + buffer); this makes the process super complicated and loses throughput.

questions.q: What lesson was boxed on the board after the evolutions?
questions.answer: There is no way to distribute and guarantee strict monotonicity (at high throughput); real solutions relax constraints: non-integer IDs and/or no monotonicity.

questions.q: Why does a single MySQL server have monotonic auto-increment IDs, and what happens in multi-master mode?
questions.answer: It's a single machine with the ID logic in the DB engine. In multi-master mode, each master is its own brain and auto-increment produces conflicts.

questions.q: What did the teacher advise when requirements say you need monotonic integer IDs?
questions.answer: Everything is a trade-off; ask critical questions and challenge whether you really need these constraints — can IDs be random (UUID/GUID), non-integer, non-monotonic? Often the requirement relaxes.

questions.q: Why do we need custom ID generation at all, given databases have auto-increment?
questions.answer: With sharded / multi-master databases, writes go to any master; two MySQL masters with auto-increment don't talk to each other and both produce 1, 2, 3, 4 — duplicates. So a custom (distributed) ID generator is needed.

questions.q: If instead of a central service you used a common database with locks to generate IDs, is that different?
questions.answer: No — that database itself is a shared service, a single machine; one and the same thing.

questions.q: Why was the static counter (rather than random values) used in the early design, and when can UUID be used?
questions.answer: Because we wanted monotonicity, and random IDs give none. If you can relax monotonicity, use a random ID like UUID — you lose ordering.

questions.q: A proposal: give each distributed ID server its own ID and append it to IDs it generates. Teacher's verdict?
questions.answer: Correct and works, but you lose monotonicity; it's a trade-off, there's no single right way.

questions.q: A proposal: on restart, read the max message ID saved in the database and continue from it. Teacher's response?
questions.answer: That is what load() already does; but it assumes every ID is written back to the DB as a row and then takes max, which is an expensive call; the generator should not assume IDs are stored.

questions.q: What problem does Amazon's ID generation solve and what is its core idea?
questions.answer: Assigning globally unique IDs (e.g. orders, plus other internal services) at high throughput; core idea is batching — instead of calling the remote service per ID, a server gets a batch (range) of IDs in one shot.

questions.q: What are the components of Amazon's ID service, as drawn?
questions.answer: API servers exposing ID-generation endpoints ('APIs for ID Svc') behind a load balancer, backed by a plain relational database holding a counter per service; service servers (orders, payments) call it through the LB.

questions.q: Do Amazon's orders/payments services need monotonic IDs?
questions.answer: No, they need only uniqueness.

questions.q: Orders server 1 boots and asks for 500 IDs, then orders server 2 asks for 500. What ranges are returned and what is the orders counter?
questions.answer: Server 1 gets [0, 500), counter becomes 500; server 2 gets [500, 1000), counter becomes 1000. Only start and end are sent, not individual IDs.

questions.q: How must the ID service update the counter to avoid two requests getting overlapping ranges?
questions.answer: In a transaction: SELECT ... FOR UPDATE (exclusive lock) then atomically add the requested count, returning old and new values as the range — like the airline check-in system; one tiny update per request.

questions.q: What does Amazon's batching enable for the order service's own databases?
questions.answer: It decouples ID generation from storage: orders DB can be sharded and scaled horizontally, every shard accepting writes, since IDs are already unique from in-memory ranges.

questions.q: What batch sizes are used in reality, and what is the trade-off in choosing the batch size?
questions.answer: 10,000, 50,000, 100,000 depending on throughput (500 was just an example). Too small = too frequent network calls; too large = losing the whole range if the server crashes.

questions.q: What does a service server do when its range is nearly exhausted?
questions.answer: It re-asks the ID service for another batch (e.g. after using 490 of 500 it fetches another 500, maybe 3000-3500) and uses it.

questions.q: Does Amazon's batching give monotonic IDs across servers? Why does it scale easily?
questions.answer: No monotonicity across servers. It scales because the single DB is the single source of truth — no gossip, just one tiny atomic update per batch request.

questions.q: Should you track exactly which IDs of a range a crashed server used so none are wasted?
questions.answer: No — the overhead of tracking every ID is massive and pointless; a 64-bit range (2^64) will never be exhausted. Think practically; we underestimate big numbers.

questions.q: How big is the gap between a million and a billion, and how many orders fit in a 4-byte integer?
questions.answer: The difference between a million and a billion is almost a billion; a 4-byte integer holds about 4 billion; go to 64 bits if that might be exhausted.

questions.q: What is a UUID's size and why do companies at scale avoid it?
questions.answer: 128 bits = 16 bytes. Indexes store the row ID for every entry, so 16-byte IDs instead of 4-byte ints bloat the index ~4x (1 GB -> 4 GB); they don't index well.

questions.q: Why does index size decide database performance?
questions.answer: Query planning and execution operate on indexes; if all indexes fit in RAM, execution happens in memory and only final rows are read from disk. If indexes spill to disk, the DB is slow no matter what.

questions.q: What is the first thing the teacher checks when asked to optimize a slow database, and how should DB RAM be provisioned?
questions.answer: Index sizes. RAM should be at least the sum of all index sizes (bare minimum).

questions.q: What advantage do UUIDs have?
questions.answer: They are random and unpredictable, good for security: sequential IDs (1, 2, 3...) exposed in URLs let anyone loop over IDs and scrape the site.

questions.q: Is UUID always wrong?
questions.answer: No. For small applications that will never hit that scale, UUID is fine; don't go for the 'best' solution unnecessarily.

questions.q: Describe the MongoDB ObjectID layout as drawn on the board.
questions.answer: 12 bytes (96 bits): epoch (4 bytes) | random (5 bytes) | counter (3 bytes); epoch on the LHS.

questions.q: What ID sizes did the teacher consider fine vs worrying?
questions.answer: MySQL auto-increment 4 bytes is tiny; 8 bytes is still doable; beyond 8 bytes worry about performance at scale.

questions.q: Why did Flickr need its own ID generation, and why not UUIDs?
questions.answer: Its database was sharded (multi-master, writes anywhere), so auto-increment everywhere would collide; it needed central generation to guarantee uniqueness. Not UUIDs because they index badly.

questions.q: Why is the database called the most brutal component of infrastructure?
questions.answer: API servers are mostly stateless and easy to scale; the database stores everything and handles the entire query load.

questions.q: What is the schema of Flickr's tickets table?
questions.answer: id bigint unsigned not null auto_increment (primary key); stub char not null default '' with a UNIQUE KEY on stub.

questions.q: What is the basic idea of using MySQL as Flickr's ID generator, and why is delete+insert not used?
questions.answer: Use auto-increment: delete and re-insert the row so the DB generates the next id. Delete then insert in a transaction is extremely costly, so use an upsert instead.

questions.q: What are MySQL's two ways of doing an upsert, and how do they differ?
questions.answer: INSERT ... ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE: tries insert, on unique-key failure runs the update clause. REPLACE INTO: on unique-key failure deletes the old row and inserts a new one — about 32x slower (teacher's own benchmark). Both atomic.

questions.q: What is the exact query Flickr fires to get a new ID?
questions.answer: INSERT INTO tickets (stub) VALUES ('a') ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE id = id + 1; — e.g. id 74 becomes 75 and is returned.

questions.q: What is the stub column for?
questions.answer: Nothing but a hard-coded dummy value: inserting 'a' deliberately violates the unique key so that the atomic update (id = id + 1) triggers. No other reason.

questions.q: In Flickr's architecture diagram, what does the photos service talk to?
questions.answer: Photos service servers call the MySQL ticket server (ID generation) to get the ID, then store the photo in a separate, sharded Photos DB.

questions.q: How did Flickr remove the single point of failure of the ticket server?
questions.answer: Two ticket servers behind a round-robin load balancer, one generating odd IDs and the other even: Server 1 auto_increment_increment = 2, offset = 1; Server 2 increment = 2, offset = 2.

questions.q: What do auto_increment_increment and auto_increment_offset mean?
questions.answer: increment = how much to add each time; offset = the starting point.

questions.q: What happens when Flickr's odd server goes down?
questions.answer: All requests go to the even server (2, 4, 6, ..., 202); ID generation continues without hiccup.

questions.q: Odd server died at 5, even reached 202, then odd comes back. What happens if nothing is reset, and is it a correctness problem?
questions.answer: Odd resumes 7, 9, 11 interleaved with 204, 206 — a huge discrepancy, but IDs remain unique; it only looks bad (aesthetics), not correctness. Monotonicity was never enforced.

questions.q: What optional reset was suggested when the odd server returns, with the board's example values?
questions.answer: Reset offsets on both DBs to MAX + BUFFER, e.g. max 202 -> 240 and 241 (then continue round robin) — starting from a safe value; purely for aesthetics.

questions.q: Who does the MAX+BUFFER reset, and how could it be automated?
questions.answer: An SRE/DevOps engineer, since a DB going down is a big event anyway. To automate: find the active server, get the max ID, add a buffer, set the values, do a quick process reboot on each server.

questions.q: Does social media need monotonic IDs?
questions.answer: Not really — not everyone needs monotonicity; it's a nice byproduct.

questions.q: What distinguishes Twitter's Snowflake from Amazon's and Flickr's approaches?
questions.answer: Amazon and Flickr are central ID services; Snowflake is decentralized ID logic — a native function/library running in app (API) servers, not a service.

questions.q: Why is it called Snowflake, and who else adopted it?
questions.answer: Every snowflake is unique. Adopted by Discord and Instagram (also Sony).

questions.q: Why are Snowflake IDs 64 bits rather than 128?
questions.answer: Storage/index efficiency at Twitter's scale: 128 bits would double the space needed.

questions.q: Give Snowflake's bit layout, in order from the left.
questions.answer: 41 bits epoch milliseconds | 10 bits machine ID | 12 bits per-machine counter (64 bits total).

questions.q: In the Snowflake diagram, where is the ID computed?
questions.answer: Inside each API server (tweet service) when it receives a tweet: it validates, computes the tweet ID with Snowflake, then stores it in the partitioned Tweets DB.

questions.q: What limit does Snowflake's 10-bit machine ID impose?
questions.answer: At most 2^10 = 1024 machines (API servers) can generate IDs.

questions.q: How many IDs can one Snowflake machine generate per millisecond, and when would a collision happen?
questions.answer: 2^12 = 4096 per ms per machine; collision only if one machine handles more than 4096 requests in one ms (~400,000+ per second), which nobody does.

questions.q: How is a Snowflake ID assembled in code?
questions.answer: Simple bit manipulation: take time, left-shift by 23, then bitwise-OR in the machine ID (shifted) and the atomically incremented counter — about three lines.

questions.q: Why did Snowflake help Twitter scale?
questions.answer: No moving parts: no central service to call or scale, no network call; request comes, ID generated locally, stored. Tweeting is extremely high-throughput.

questions.q: What does 'roughly sortable' mean for Snowflake, and what does it enable?
questions.answer: First 41 bits are epoch ms so IDs move forward each ms; within a ms order is by machine ID. You can get objects before/after a time or ID from the ID itself — great for pagination.

questions.q: What are the two ways to paginate, with the SQL for limit-offset?
questions.answer: 1) Limit-offset (skip-limit): SELECT * FROM tweets WHERE user_id = ? LIMIT 10 OFFSET 0, then OFFSET 10, 20... 2) ID-based: fetch rows with id > last seen id LIMIT 10 (Twitter uses since_id).

questions.q: Why is limit-offset pagination slow at depth?
questions.answer: The DB must evaluate the result set up to the requested point, skip that many and then return the page, so cost grows linearly with depth.

questions.q: Give a use case for deep pagination at Twitter beyond scrolling a profile.
questions.answer: Batch jobs, e.g. computing trending topics over the last hour of tweets — iterating over millions of rows.

questions.q: Describe ID-limit pagination steps as shown in the MongoDB article.
questions.answer: 1. Fetch a page; 2. take the id of the last document; 3. retrieve documents with _id greater than that id: db.students.find({_id: {$gt: last_id}}).limit(10).

questions.q: When does ID-based pagination work?
questions.answer: When IDs are comparable — auto-increment, MongoDB ObjectIDs, Snowflake, anything with time on the left; and tables are physically stored ordered by primary key.

questions.q: What did the benchmark graph show?
questions.answer: skip-limit (blue) time grows linearly with depth; id-limit (green) is constant. For small depth (up to ~500-600) they're comparable. A spike was due to disk throttling.

questions.q: Why is ID-based pagination constant time?
questions.answer: Data is stored in a B+ tree ordered by primary key: log n to reach the ID, then a sequential scan — the same cost at any depth.

questions.q: What is the limitation of ID-based pagination?
questions.answer: You can't apply complex/advanced WHERE clauses; so don't replace all pagination with it.

questions.q: What did Discord change in Snowflake and why?
questions.answer: Same structure as Twitter, but a custom epoch starting at the first second of 2015 (when the company began) instead of 1 Jan 1970, to get a larger range for the 41-bit time.

questions.q: What is Sony's Snowflake called and where is it?
questions.answer: Sonyflake, a Go implementation, open sourced on GitHub.

questions.q: What benefits of Snowflake did the board list?
questions.answer: No moving part; no service; just a function call (library); no extra load on DB. Logic handled by API servers.

questions.q: What was the teacher's view on building a microservice for ID generation?
questions.answer: Good engineers don't reflexively build microservices; look for the most efficient solution — often an overkill. Keep things simple; make data-driven decisions.

questions.q: How did the teacher know his disk throttled during the benchmark?
questions.answer: He had Prometheus node exporter running, exporting the disk IO utilization metric, which hit 100%.

questions.q: Does ID-based pagination work for NoSQL databases?
questions.answer: Depends on the storage engine: works where data has locality / sequential scanning (MongoDB, DynamoDB); not with completely decentralized hash-based storage.

questions.q: What limit does Elasticsearch place on limit-offset pagination?
questions.answer: A hard limit of 10,000 documents for offset pagination; beyond that it errors and tells you to use the cursor/scroll API.

questions.q: What is the counter in Snowflake?
questions.answer: A per-server (per-machine) counter atomically incremented on each ID generation — the static counter from the start.

questions.q: Epoch is just a number — how does a custom epoch save range?
questions.answer: The 41 bits hold milliseconds since the epoch; starting from 1970 wastes decades already elapsed. Subtracting a custom start time makes the counter start from zero, giving ~45 years of fresh range.

questions.q: What were Instagram's requirements for IDs?
questions.answer: IDs sortable by time (filtering, batch processing, pagination), about 64 bits to be efficient on indexes, and no new service.

questions.q: Where does Instagram generate Snowflake IDs, versus Twitter?
questions.answer: Twitter: in API servers. Instagram: in the database during INSERT.

questions.q: Give Instagram's ID bit layout.
questions.answer: 41 bits epoch ms since 1 Jan 2011 | 13 bits DB shard ID | 10 bits per-shard sequence number.

questions.q: What are logical shards and physical servers at Instagram?
questions.answer: Physical DB servers are the actual DB machines (10-15); logical shards are databases created with CREATE DATABASE inside them (thousands, up to 2^13 = 8192), each with the same tables/schemas but different data.

questions.q: What is the advantage of logical shards?
questions.answer: Rebalancing is easy: dump a hot logical database and load it onto another/new physical server; no row-by-row extraction. Horizontal scaling becomes easy.

questions.q: What is the operational cost of many logical databases?
questions.answer: Migrations (e.g. adding a column) must run on every logical database on every physical server — thousands of times.

questions.q: How is the photos table's id column defined at Instagram?
questions.answer: id bigint not null default insta5.next_id() — a stored procedure invoked when no ID is provided on insert.

questions.q: What variables does insta5.next_id declare?
questions.answer: epoch = 1314220021721 (1 Jan 2011 in ms), seq_id, now_ms, shard_id = 5 (hard-coded per shard; a function per database).

questions.q: How is the sequence part computed in next_id?
questions.answer: nextval('insta5.table_id_seq') % 1024 — an atomically incrementing DB sequence, limited to 10 bits.

questions.q: Write the three lines that assemble Instagram's ID.
questions.answer: result := (now_ms - epoch) << 23; result := result | (shard_id << 10); result := result | seq_id;

questions.q: Why is Instagram's in-DB approach efficient?
questions.answer: No ID logic on the API side; inserts are normal inserts without an ID, the default calls the function — all offloaded to the DB.

questions.q: Is table_id_seq a column?
questions.answer: No — it is a sequencer (sequence) object; auto-increment columns create one implicitly, and you can create any named sequence explicitly.

questions.q: What scaling limit does Instagram remove versus Twitter?
questions.answer: Twitter is limited to 2^10 API servers by the machine ID; Instagram's API servers are unlimited; limit is ~8192 logical databases.

questions.q: How do machines get their machine IDs in Snowflake?
questions.answer: Assigned at startup, e.g. by ZooKeeper; within the same ms the smaller machine ID sorts first.

questions.q: Does Snowflake guarantee strict monotonic inserts? When should you use auto-increment?
questions.answer: No. If you need strict monotonicity (e.g. a bank listing transactions), use auto-increment; social media doesn't care.

questions.q: How do the distributed ID servers gossip?
questions.answer: Not specified; any gossip protocol or own: network calls to check the greatest IDs, agree on a value plus buffer — consensus is the key. Lamport clocks aren't for gossip.

questions.q: Could Amazon's ID service push ID ranges onto a queue?
questions.answer: Yes — batches pushed to the queue; the queue's atomic reads replace the DB's atomicity. Any atomic system works (DynamoDB, Redis).

questions.q: Why did the benchmark graph spike then drop?
questions.answer: Other processes on his local machine contended for resources.

questions.q: Should the sequence be kept only in cache?
questions.answer: No — it must be persistent, else it restarts from zero after a DB reboot; the DB optimizes flushes itself.

questions.q: Must pagination IDs be numeric?
questions.answer: No — string IDs are stored and compared lexicographically, still comparable.

questions.q: Must Snowflake requests be round-robin? Can monotonicity be guaranteed?
questions.answer: Not necessary; monotonicity can't be guaranteed in a distributed setup (clocks drift) — accept rough sortability; strict needs lower throughput.
